questiontext.text:
What is the value of the dictionary d after these statements run?

d = {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
d['a'] = 3

feedback.text: Each key can only appear once in a dictionary.
The second assignment statement changes the value associated with the key 'a'.

answer.text: These statements cause a runtime error

feedback.text: This code runs without causing an error.
The second assignment statement updates the value associated with the key 'a'.

questiontext.text:
What happens when the following statements run?

d1 = {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
d2 = {d1: 3}

answer.text: They add d1 as a key in d2.

feedback.text: Dictionaries are mutable, so they are not hashable, so they cannot appear as a key in a dictionary.

questiontext.text:
A dictionary is like a list, but more general. Which words complete this sentence?

"The _ of a dictionary are like the indices of a list, and the _ of a dictionary are like the elements of a list."

feedback.text: An item is a key-value pair, so it's not like an index. The keys play the role of the indices.
This is backwards: we use a key to look up a value, the way we use an index to look up an element.
The keys are like indices, but an item is a whole key-value pair, not the thing you look up.
We use a key to look up its value, just as we use an index to look up an element. Indices have to be integers, but keys can be (almost) any type.
